message: The fixture was serviced three days ago, so I suspect calibration drift at Station 7. I would recalibrate before changing the software.
The most likely cause is the r4.2 diagnostic timing change. Recommended action: contain affected units and roll Station 7 back to r4.1 for confirmation.
That recommendation is too categorical. A software deployment and a failure spike occurring together do not establish causation. What rules out the fixture?
The timing and retest pattern are more consistent with a software-related false failure than with calibration drift.
Which retest pattern? I need the stations, sample size, and result before approving rollback.
Seven of 30 units failed under r4.2 at Station 7. After rollback to r4.1, all 30 passed. The seven failed units also passed the downstream electrical bench.
That makes a physical connector defect unlikely. Calibration drift could still produce false failures, but the rollback result shifts me toward the software hypothesis.
Release r4.2 reduced the response timeout from 180 ms to 120 ms. Station 6 remained on r4.1 and its failure rate remained stable, despite using the same connector batch.
The temporal discontinuity, cross-station contrast, rollback result, and timeout mechanism jointly favor H3. I approve containment and rollback, but want a blinded confirmation sample before release.

Agreed. Run 50 affected units in randomized order under r4.1 and r4.2, keep fixture settings fixed, and compare false-failure rates against the independent bench. Escalate only if the software contrast fails to reproduce.

I estimate H3 at 0.87 and recommend A3. Evidence map: E1 links the increase to r4.2 deployment; E2 provides a same-batch station contrast; E5 shows reversal after rollback; E6 indicates false positives; and E7 supplies a timeout mechanism. E4 weakly supports H1, so fixture drift is not impossible. The critical uncertainty is whether the rollback sample reproduces under randomized order.
The reversal and the unaffected r4.1 station substantially weaken H1. I now favor H3, but I want to separate the software effect from order and warm-up effects with an interleaved confirmation test.

Use 50 affected units, randomized between r4.1 and r4.2 while holding fixture parameters constant. Verify each EOL result on the independent bench. This tests the software contrast and protects against fixture and sequence confounds.
Agreed. We will accept H3 provisionally if r4.2 produces a materially higher false-failure rate than r4.1 and the independent bench remains negative. Otherwise we reopen H1.
That rule is appropriate. A falsifier for H3 would be comparable failure rates under both releases after randomization, especially if failures track fixture position rather than software version.
Containment is justified because rollback is reversible and the present evidence indicates false rejects rather than escaped defects. We should preserve all logs to test the 120 ms mechanism.
The joint plan now covers diagnosis, production risk, and falsification: contain, roll back, randomize the software comparison, verify externally, and retain latency traces.
Final decision: A3. H3 is the leading explanation, not a certainty. The plan distinguishes immediate containment from causal confirmation and specifies when to return to the calibration hypothesis.
Decision recorded with H3 at 0.92, A3 selected, H1 retained as the principal alternative, and the randomized release comparison defined as the next discriminating intervention.
